main.text: [II, 676] [col. 109] Chapter XVI.

Twelve passages of the Prophets which some interpreters refer to the gallinaceous kind. I. Levit. XIV, 4. II. 1 Reg. IV, 23. var. V, 3. III. 2 Reg. XVII, 30. IV. Iob. III, 7. V. Iob. XXXVIII, 32. VI. Iob. XXXVIII, 36. VII. Iob. XXXIX, 13. VIII. Ps. L, 11. IX. Ps. LXXX, 14. X. Prov. XXX, 31. XI. Eccles. XII, 4. var. 6. XII. Esaj. XXII, 17.

The cock is called ديك [dīk] dic in Arabic, and ܬܪܢܓܠ tarnegol in Syriac; both names, if I am not mistaken, are very old. [col. 110] For traces of the former appear in the Hebrew דוכיפת dukiphat, by which Moses names the hoopoe; a word, as it seems, compounded of דוך and כיפה, so that it means cock of the rocks, or rock-dwelling cock, as we shall show elsewhere. And from the Syriac ܬܪܢܓܠ tarnegol, I think, the Phoenicians who had come with Cadmus into Boeotia gave its name to Tanagra, a very ancient city of Boeotia, home of the Tanagraean cocks. These are praised as most pugnacious by Varro, Columella, Pliny, Pausanias, Hesychius, Suidas and others, whose passages we have cited in our [col. 111] Chanaan, book 1, ch. 16. That is, the city itself was called Tarnegol or Tarnegal by the Phoenicians after those cocks. And the Greeks, dropping the final l, as in Ἀννίβα [Anniba] and Ἀσδρούβα [Asdrouba], made from Tarnegal first Tarnegam, then Tanagram, by the transposition of a single letter. Thus the city of Tanagra is the city of the cock, or of cocks. Their renown was so great that among the ancients cock and Ταναγραῖος [Tanagraios] are almost interchangeable, as if all cocks must have originated from Tanagra. Hence in Lucian's Cock, Micyllus says to Pythagoras, who has been transformed into a cock: Εἰπὲ δὲ ὅμως, ὦ Μνησάρχου παῖ, ὅπως ἡμῖν ἀντὶ μὲν ἀνθρώπου ὄρνις, ἀντὶ δὲ Σαμίου Ταναγραῖος ἀναπέφηνας· [Eipe de homōs, ō Mnēsarchou pai, hopōs hēmin anti men anthrōpou ornis, anti de Samiou Tanagraios anapephēnas] Yet explain, son of Mnesarchus, how it has come about that you have appeared to us as a bird instead of a man, and as a Tanagraean instead of a Samian. Tanagraean, that is, cock, תרנגול. Meanwhile, neither name for the cock appears in the Prophetic books. Nor is it sufficiently known what the ancient Hebrews called the cock; although interpreters refer many passages of the Prophets to the gallinaceous kind, but on conjectures that are not certain enough, as will be clear to anyone who runs through them, as what follows will make plain.

I. The first passage, as far as I recall, is Levit. XIV, 4., where the leper who has been cleansed is commanded to offer to God δύο ὀρνίθια ζῶντα καθαρὰ [dyo ornithia zōnta kathara], that is, as some would have it, two living clean little hens. Origen, Homily 8 on Leviticus: He commands that two living hens be taken for him who is cleansed. And a little later: These two hens also seem to me here to bear a certain likeness to the two [II, 677] goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent out into the wilderness: for so here too, of the two hens one is sacrificed and the other is released into the field. And again: He who is purged of leprosy and offers hens. Likewise: Because the Lawgiver commands that on the same day on which he is purged two hens be taken, let there be a hidden understanding, through which the purification of the sinner is effected, of which it is written, “How often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen,” etc. Since these words are ἀσύνδετα [asyndeta], they seem to need reading thus: Because the Lawgiver commands that on the same day on which he is purged two hens be taken, let there be a hidden understanding of the hen, through which, etc. That is, by those hens he wants Christ to be signified, who in the Gospel compares himself to a hen. Hence the addition: The hen shall be killed in an earthen vessel into which running water has been put, so that water too may be taken for the purification, and the fullness of the mystery may be fulfilled in the water and the blood which is said to have come forth from the side of the Saviour. And much more about this same hen can be read in what follows. In the ninth volume of the Works of Jerome, the author of the thirty-ninth Epistle, On the various kinds of leprosies, following the same view, says: But why are two hens commanded to be offered for the cleansing of leprosies? The two hens seem to indicate the soul and the flesh: but one hen, he says, you shall kill, the other you shall wash and release, etc. Yet in the Hebrew text nothing is said of hens: God merely commands that in the purification of leprosy שתי צפורים be taken, two birds (or two little birds, or two sparrows), which the Greeks rendered not badly as δύο ὀρνίθια [dyo ornithia], but with an ambiguous word, which in the age of the Fathers meant only hens, or for the most part hens. Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 4, where he treats of the gallinaceous kind: Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ ὄρνιθας, καὶ ὀρνίθια νῦν μόνον ἡ συνήθεια καλεῖ τὰς θηλείας· [alla mēn kai ornithas, kai ornithia nyn monon hē synētheia kalei tas thēleias] Now indeed the custom has prevailed that only the females of cocks (that is, hens) are called ὄρνιθες [ornithes] and ὀρνίθια [ornithia]. This gave occasion to the error. Yet Plutarch, nearly contemporary with Athenaeus, says in the Artaxerxes that the rhyndax is μικρὸν ἐν Πέρσαις ὀρνίθιον [mikron en Persais ornithion], that is, a small little bird among the Persians. And that in the Law δύο ὀρνίθια καθαρὰ [dyo ornithia kathara] are two clean little birds ought to have been clear enough even to those ignorant of the Hebrew language. For the lawgiver would not have said two clean hens. That epithet would have been pointless, since every hen is clean.

II. The second passage is 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.], where among Solomon's provisions [col. 112] are reckoned ברבורים אבוסים, that is, תרנגולין פטומין, fattened cocks, as it is found in Selomo, whom Pagninus follows. Likewise for Pomarius and Aquinas ברבור barbur is תרנגול סריס, a castrated cock, that is, a capon. Nor do the Greek translators depart far from this; here they have ἐκτὸς ὀρνίθων ἐκλεκτῶν νομάδων [ektos ornithōn eklektōn nomadōn], besides choice pasture-fed hens. I prefer this to rendering it, as others do, besides birds, etc. For although ὄρνιθες [ornithes] are often birds in general, yet for the Greek translators, as for the Evangelists, a bird is ὄρνεον [orneon], and a hen is ὄρνις [ornis]. Moreover, ὄρνις νομὰς [ornis nomas] is nothing other than a fattened or pasture-fed hen. In Nicander's Alexipharmaca, line [II, 678] 295, there is βοσκὰς ὀρταλὶς [boskas ortalis], where the Scholiast has νομὰς ὄρνις [nomas ornis], the very words of the Greek translators. And in Artemidorus's Ὀψαρτυτικά [Opsartytika], as cited by Athenaeus, book 14, chapter 23: Νομάδα παχεῖαν ἕψε, καὶ νεοσσοὺς τῶν ἤδη κοκκυζόντων [Nomada pacheian hepse, kai neossous tōn ēdē kokkyzontōn]; Boil a fat pasture-fed hen, and, of the chicks, those that already crow. So it must be rendered, not, as the translator most ineptly has it, a fat dove, etc., and of the chicks those that still peep. For the subject is a mattya to be made from a hen. Accordingly it is immediately added: Εἶτ᾽ ἐξελὼν τὰ λάχανα εἰς τρυβλίον, καὶ τῆς ὄρνιθος τῶν κρεῶν ἐπιθεὶς [Eit᾽ exelōn ta lachana eis trublion, kai tēs ornithos tōn kreōn epitheis]; Then taking out the vegetables, put them into a dish, and placing the hen's meat on them. And ἤδη [ēdē] does not mean still, but already. Nor is κοκκύζειν [kokkyzein] proper to doves, but to cocks, as is clear from Aristophanes, Aristotle, Theocritus, Aelian and Lucian. For it is an onomatopoeic word, like the vernacular coq for the cock, which we name thus from its crowing. Finally, νομὰς [nomas] is a hen, yet not a Numidian one, as the most learned commentator would have it, but a pasture-fed one. Others call them σιτιστὰς [sitistas] or σιτευτὰς [siteutas]. Athenaeus, book 14, chapter 21: Σιτιστῶν δὲ ὀρνίθων μὲν μνημονεύει Μάτρων ἐν ταῖς Παρῳδίαις οὕτως [Sitistōn de ornithōn men mnēmoneuei Matrōn en tais Parōdiais houtōs],
Ὣς ἔφαθ᾽, οἱ δ᾽ ἐγέλασσαν, ἐπήνεγκάν τ᾽ ἐπὶ τούτῳ Σιτευτὰς ὄρνιθας ἐπ᾽ ἀργυρέοισι πίναξι· [Hōs ephath᾽, hoi d᾽ egelassan, epēnenkan t᾽ epi toutō Siteutas ornithas ep᾽ argyreoisi pinaxi]

Matron mentions fattened hens thus in his Parodies: When he had said this, they laughed, and then brought in fattened hens on silver platters. I say fattened hens with Metellus, the Pontifex Maximus, whose words are in the description of the pontifical dinner in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 3, chapter 13: Before the dinner, sea urchins, raw oysters, as many as they wished, giant clams, spondyli, a thrush, asparagus, and beneath it a fattened hen. Nor did Pliny mean anything else by the term altilia when he said of the seed of the tamarisk, book 24, chapter 9: Applied with the fat of fattened fowls to boils. Cato had said pascales; whence Festus: Both sheep and hens are called pascales, because they graze about everywhere. Pascales, that is, νομάδες [nomades], as altiles are σιτισταὶ [sitistai] or σιτευταί [siteutai]. Thus in the view of the Greeks ברבורים אבוסים are pasture-fed or fattened hens. And that some of the older Hebrews held the same view is found in Selomo. This, however, can by no means be held as certain and established, since there is no word whose meaning is more disputed, as we shall show below in a chapter devoted to that word.

III. The third passage about the cock is 2 Reg. XVII, 30., where, of the peoples transferred by Shalmaneser from Assyria into Judaea, the Babylonians are said to have worshipped סכות־בנות Succoth-Benoth, and the Cuthaeans Nergal. Succoth-Benoth, that is, the hen with her chicks; and Nergal, that is, the cock, as the Hebrews would have it. For so the Talmudists in Sanhedrin, chapter 7, folio 63b: אנשי בבל עשו את סכות־בנות ומאי ניהו תרנגולת אנשי כותה עשו נרגל ומאי ניהו תרנגול, The men of Babel made [II, 679] Succoth-Benoth. What (idol) was this? A hen. The men of Cutha made Nergal. What was that? A cock. Solomon Jarchi: סכות־בנות דמות תרנגולת עם אפרוחיה נרגל דמות תרנגול, Succoth-Benoth was the image of a hen with her chicks, and Nergal the image of a cock. Kimchi: ובדברי רז״ל סכות־בנות זה תרנגולת היו עובדים והיה שמה סכות בנות וכמו שקורין לתרנגול סכוי כן היו [col. 113] קורין לתרנגולת סכות ובנות פירוש עם אפרוחיה נרגל זה תרנגולת הבר, In the words of our masters of blessed memory, Succoth-benoth is the hen, which they worshipped under this name. For just as they called the cock שכוי secui, so they called the hen סכות succoth. And the added benoth signifies that she was with her chicks. And nergal is the wild hen. The most trifling of trifles. Literally, סכות בנות Succoth-benoth are tents of daughters, or of girls. So when the Babylonians are said to have made Succoth-benoth, I understand that they built a shrine of goddesses who were called בנות benoth, that is, girls, just as the Greeks called Proserpina κόρην [korēn], that is, girl. So in Amos V, 26. סכות מלככם, the tabernacle of your king, that is, the shrine of your idol ^{(1)}. And what נרגל Nergal is, I do not know, except that almost the same name as this idol belongs to a species of palm called even today by the Persians, Arabs and Indians نارجيل [nārjīl] nergil, of which they tell wonders. It must therefore be considered whether the idol of the Persians could have been named from this palm, as in Syria ܪܡܘܢ Rimmon was from pomegranates, 2 Reg. V, 18.

IV. The fourth passage is Iob. III, 7. There, for the words of Job in which he curses the night in which he was born, Let no רננה, song, come in it, the Chaldee has: לא תעול רננא דתרנגול ברא למקלסה בה, Let not the song of the wild cock come to give praise in it. This does not concern the cock in general, but a fabulous cock of prodigious size, which we shall treat in the treatise On the Ostrich. And the same translator says more about it in the passages that follow, taken from Job and the Psalms.

V. The fifth passage is Iob. XXXVIII, 32., where the Chaldee has, in the Venice and Basel editions, וזגתא על אפרחהא תדברנון, And will you lead the hen with her chicks? Word for word, upon her chicks. But upon the chicks means with the chicks, as in Deuter. XXII, 6. You shall not take the mother upon the young, i.e. with the young. Hen is זגתא, as in the Talmudic tractate Bechoroth, ch. 1, fol. 8. 2: איותי לה תרי ביעי אמר ליה הי דוגתא אוכמתי והי דוגתא חיוורתי, When two eggs were brought, he said to him: That egg is of a black hen, and this one of a white hen. Nor is זגתא pronounced Zagtha, as [II, 680] some think, but Zaggatha. For it belongs to the verbs that double the second radical, like the Arabic name of the hen, دجاجة [dajāja] degiagia, which they derive from the verb دج [dajja] daggia, that is, to walk gently. I think it is formed from the bird's call, which different people render differently. Or else from the Chaldee זגג, with Zain and Daleth interchanged, which is customary in those languages. For the rest, in the paraphrase of Job, beware of understanding the common hen. For the subject is the celestial one, which in the vernacular is called pullicenaria [the Hen-and-Chickens], by the Greeks Πλειὰς [Pleias] or Πλειάδες [Pleiades], and by the Latins Vergiliae ^{(2)}. But in the Hebrew it is ועיש על בניה תנחם, and will you lead עיש with her sons? And in that passage עיש is plainly something other than the Pleiades. Namely, עיש is the same as עש in Iob. IX, 9. And עש as is formed by ἀφαίρεσιν [aphairesin] from the Arabic نعش [naʿsh] nas, as an initial N often drops out. Thus גיא gia, splendour, is formed from נגה naga, to shine; גר gar, river, from נגר nagar, to flow; שיא si, or שאת seeth, elevation, from נשה nasa, to lift up; שיג sig, pursuit, from נשג nasag, to pursue or to overtake. Further, for the Arabs نعش [naʿsh] nas is first a bier, as in Luc. VII, 14. and in Eutychius of Alexandria, p. 277; then the constellation of the Bear. Thus among the astrologers النعش الكبري [al-naʿsh al-kubrī] is the greater bier, that is, Ursa Major; النعش الصغري [al-naʿsh al-ṣughrī] the lesser bier, that is, Ursa Minor. For the four stars, [col. 114] arranged in a square, are taken by them as a bier, or sarcophagus, on which a corpse is carried out. And the three that follow (for us the tail of the Bear) are for them daughters, or sons, who accompany the funeral. Alcamus: بنات نعش الكبري سبعة كواكب اربعة منها نعش وثلاث بنات [banāt naʿsh al-kubrī sabʿat kawākib arbaʿa minhā naʿsh wa-thalāth banāt] The daughters of the greater bier, of which four are the bier and three are daughters. And elsewhere: الحية كواكب ما بين الغرقدين وبنات نعش [al-ḥayya kawākib mā bayna al-gharqadayn wa-banāt naʿsh] The Serpent (or Dragon) is stars that lie between alpharkadin (the polar stars) and the daughters of the bier. Again elsewhere: [II, 681] الصبا ريح مهبها من مطلع الثريا الي بنات نعش [al-ṣabā rīḥ mahabbuhā min maṭlaʿ al-thurayyā ilā banāt naʿsh] Saba, a wind blowing from the rising of the Pleiades to the daughters of the bier, that is, Caecias. Giauhari notes that among the poets one sometimes reads بنى نعش [banī naʿsh] sons of the bier, and of each one individually in the singular ابن نعش [ibn naʿsh] son of the bier ^{(3)}. Hence clear light is shed on the passage of Job we are dealing with: Will you lead עיש, the bier, with her sons? ^{(4)} And although the reason for this expression escaped the interpreters, Aben Ezra nevertheless saw rightly that the subject is the constellation of seven stars in the north, which some call the Bear, others the Wain, others Helice, others the Septentriones. Nor do I dwell on the Talmudists, for some of whom עש is זנב טלה, the tail of the Ram; for others רישא דעגלא, the head of the Bull, in the tractate Berachoth, fol. 58. b. The Glossator tries to reconcile these opinions, because ראש השור סמוך לזנב טלה שכן הסדר טלה שור תאומים, The head of the Bull is joined to the tail of the Ram, since this is the order of the signs: Ram, Bull, Twins, etc. Nor is it hidden from me why the Chaldee wanted עיש to be the Pleiades. ערש in Hebrew means to come together and to be gathered, Ioel IV, 11. So it seemed to him that this constellation was called עיש as if from coming together, just as in Greek it is called Πλειὰς [Pleias], ὡς ἐκ πλειόνων ἀςέρων οὖσα [hōs ek pleionōn asterōn ousa], and in Arabic ثري [thry] from the same idea, for ثرا [tharā] means to be multiplied. But why do the Greek translators render Καὶ ἕσπερον ἐπὶ κόμης αὐτοῦ ἄξεις αὐτὸν [Kai hesperon epi komēs autou axeis auton], And the evening star, will you lead it by its hair? For בניה her sons they read בנית, hair. And they derived עיש, or עש, from عشي [ʿashī], which is what the Arabs call evening. In the Vulgate the old editions have And do you make the evening star rise over the ends of the earth? And the new ones over [II, 682] the sons of the earth. But I think both are corrupt. For one should read And do you make the evening star rise over its sons? That tune [its], otherwise rare in that version, is nevertheless found in 2 Reg. II, 20. and 3 Reg. XIII, 13. 14. and XVIII, 17. The scribes corrupted the passage because they did not grasp what the sons of the evening star were. But the corruption is very old, for it had already taken root in the age of Gregory the Great, who evidently read sons of the earth, in book 29 on Job, chapter 17.

VI. The sixth passage, Iob. XXXVIII, 36., reads thus in Hebrew: Who has put בטחות wisdom in the reins, or given לשכוי understanding to the heart? In Scripture, namely, heart and reins are frequently joined, as being, in the mind of the Hebrews, the proper seat of thoughts. For examples see Psalm. VII, 10. and XXVI, 2. and LXXIII, 21., Proverb. XXIII, 15. 26. Ierem. XI, 20. and XVII, 10. and XX, 12. So also in this passage. But whereas the reins are commonly called כליות and the heart לב, here each is given another name, and a more poetic one. The reins are called טוחות tuchoth [col. 115] here and in Psal. LI, 8., from the verb טוח, which means to smear and to coat, because the reins are smeared and coated with fat, as has already been proved elsewhere. The heart, on the other hand, is called שכוי, from the verb שכה, which means to think and to imagine. Hence also שכיות are pictures and images, Es. II, 16., and אבן משכית is a painted stone, Levit. XXVI, 1.; and משכיות לבב, imaginations of the heart, Psal. LXXIII, 7.; and במשכיתו, in his imagination, Prov. XVIII, 11. Although these things are clear and plain, and confirmed in explicit words by the most learned of the Hebrews, namely Kimchi, Aben Ezra and R. Levi, others have nevertheless chosen to interpret the words of Job just cited thus: Who has put wisdom in the reins, or given understanding to the cock? As if שכוי in that place meant cock. The first author of this fiction was a certain R. Simeon, son of Lakis, whose words are cited as follows in the Talmudic tractate On the beginning of the year, fol. 26a: כשהלכתי לתחום קן נשריא הוו קורין לכלה נינפי ולתרנגול שכוי, When I was travelling through the territory of Kennasaria, there they called a bride nympha, and a cock secui. In the same place others trifle that a bride is called nympha because Mount Zion is called beautiful in נוף noph, that is, in situation, Psal. XLVIII, 3. (For the Greek word νύμφη [nymphē] escaped these circumcised doctors.) They add that the cock is called שכוי secui from the passage of Job we have mentioned. From so impure a source the error at once spread more widely and found many defenders. Among them the Chaldee translator gives a twofold interpretation of this passage: one sound and true, מן יהב ללבא בינתא, Who gave understanding to the heart?; the other Talmudic, מן יהב לתרנגולא ברא בינתא למקלסא למרה, Who gave the wild cock understanding, to praise his Lord? And R. Selomo asserts both thus: למכוי זה תרנגול לשון חכמים וי״א הלב, Secui in the language of the sages means cock, although others explain it as heart. And Aquinas, after quoting the passage of Job: יש מפרשים תרנגול והוא שגור מאד במשנה, There are some who interpret it as cock, which is very common in the Mishnah. Kimchi proves this at some length, although he [II, 683] is of the other opinion. Accordingly, in the Prayer Book, printed and reprinted so many times, this prayer is found among the morning prayers: בא״י אמ״ה אשר נתן לשכוי בינה להבין בין יום ובין לילה, Blessed art thou, O Lord our God, King of the world, who hast given τῷ [tō] secui (that is, the cock) understanding to distinguish day from night. In this prayer the allusion to the passage of Job is evident. And Jerome, no doubt persuaded by that Jew whom he had as his teacher, rendered the same passage thus: Who has put wisdom in the inward parts of man? or who has given understanding to the cock? He thus joins in the same verse two ἀσύνδετα [asyndeta], namely the wisdom of man with the natural instinct of the cock, by which it is prompted to crow at fixed hours. And this in a book in which the two hemistichs of a verse are almost always ἀντίστροφα [antistropha]. I shall note in passing the origin of the version of the Greeks, which might seem entirely foreign: Τίς δὲ ἔδωκεν γυναιξὶν ὑφάσματος σοφίαν, ἢ ποικιλτικὴν ἐπιστήμην; [Tis de edōken gynaixin hyphasmatos sophian, ē poikiltikēn epistēmēn?] And who gave women wisdom in weaving, or skill in embroidery? For בטחות, in the reins, they read בטוות, in spinning women; and לשכות, for painting or variegating, for לשכוי, to the heart. Written that way, the Hebrew is rendered word for word: Who has put wisdom in spinning women? Or who has given them understanding for painting, or variegating? But the Greek translators turned the skill of spinning into ὑφάσματος σοφίαν [hyphasmatos sophian], because νῆμα [nēma] and ὕφασμα [hyphasma] are often used interchangeably, as it would be easy to prove from Homer, Hesychius and Eustathius.

VII. The seventh passage, Iob. XXXIX, 13. (var. 16.), כנף רננים נעלסה, is rendered thus by the Chaldee: גדפא דתרנגולא דמשבחא ומקלסא, The wing of the cock, which praises and [col. 116] celebrates. They refer this to the cock discussed above. But in the chapter On the Ostrich we have proved at length that these words must be rendered thus: The wing of the ostriches exults. Accordingly this passage too is beside the point.

VIII. The eighth is Psal. L, 11., where the Hebrew has, I know every bird of the mountains, וזיז שדי עמדי, and the ziz of the field is with me. And the Chaldee: Before me are open all the kinds of birds that fly in the air of the heavens, ותרנגול ברא דקרצולי שרין בארעא ורישיה מטי בשמיא, and the wild cock, whose legs stand on the ground, and whose head reaches the heavens.

IX. And the ninth is Psal. LXXX, 14., where for the Hebrew וזיז שדה ירענה, And the ziz of the field has grazed it down, the Chaldee again has ותרנגולא ברא יתפרנס מנה, And the wild cock shall feed on it. As though the Hebrew זיז ziz meant a cock, and indeed that cock of which so much is said. But in the chapter On the Boar we have shown that זיז ziz in Hebrew is a wild beast, and is so called from movement, like the Greek κνώδαλα [knōdala] and κινώπετα [kinōpeta]. Thus neither of these passages has anything about the cock.

[II, 684] X. The tenth passage is Prov. XXX, 31., where Solomon periphrastically calls some animal that walks in stately fashion זרזיר מתנים, girded in the loins. For verses 29, 30, 31 run thus: There are three of fine gait; indeed four that step handsomely. The lion, strongest of animals, who turns back before no one; the one girded in the loins; and the he-goat; and the king, against whom no one rises up. And there the words זרזיר מתנים, that is, girded in the loins, are rendered with remarkable freedom by the Greeks as ἀλεκτὼρ ἐμπεριπατῶν θηλείαις εὐψύχως [alektōr emperipatōn thēleiais eupsychōs], a cock walking briskly among the females. And by the Arabic translator as الديك اذا تمشا بين الاناث من الدجاج بطيبة النفس [al-dīk idhā tamashshā bayna al-ināth min al-dajāj bi-ṭībat al-nafs], The cock, when he walks among the female hens with briskness of spirit. And also by the Syriac as ܐܒܟܐ ܕܡܙܕܪܟܠ ܒܝܢܬ ܬܪܢܓܠܬܐ, A cock walking proudly among the hens. If you compare these with the Chaldee version, from which they were derived, you will find that a threefold error has crept into it. For the Chaldee version reads אכבא דמודרז בינת תרנגולי, for which one should write אבכא דמזדרכל בינת תרנגולן. By the Chaldeans and Syrians the cock is called ܬܪܢܓܘܠ tarnegol. Nowhere otherwise, as far as I remember, except in this one passage, where for cock the Syriac has ܐܒܟܐ abacha, and the Chaldee אכבא achaba. Accordingly Baal Aruch unconcernedly passed over the word אכבא achaba. And Elias professes that he does not understand it. Others explain it as cock. I prefer to write it with the Syriac ܐܒܟܐ abacha rather than with the Chaldee אכבא achaba. For if it is written אכבא achaba, it will be of unknown origin. But ܐܒܟܐ abacha is from the verb אבך abach, whose Hithphael התאבך hithabach means to be lifted up and to be borne aloft, Es. IX, 18. Hence the cock seems to have been called ܐܒܟܐ abacha, a most apt name, and one that exactly expresses the nature of this bird. For, if you except the peacock, no bird is prouder than the cock. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 21, after treating of the pride of the peacock, says: Next to them, these night-watchmen of ours also have a sense of glory, whom nature brought forth to rouse mortals to their work and to break their sleep. And a little later: But if the palm (in the fight) falls to them, they at once crow in victory and proclaim themselves the masters. The vanquished hides in silence and bears servitude with difficulty. And yet the common flock too struts just as proudly, with neck held high and crests lofty, and alone among birds often looks up at the sky, raising aloft also its sickle-shaped tail. These are so many signs of pride. And Aelian, Hist. book 4, ch. 29: Κρατήσας δὲ γαῦρός ἐστι, καὶ ὑψαυχενεῖν, καὶ [col. 117] κυδρουμένῳ ἔοικεν [Kratēsas de gauros esti, kai hypsauchenein, kai kydroumenō eoiken] (read ὑψαυχενῶν, καὶ κυδρουμένῳ ἐοικὼς [hypsauchenōn, kai kydroumenō eoikōs]), When he has won he is proud, with neck erect, and like one exulting. And Philes, chapter 12,

Ἀλεκτρυὼν μέν τοι γε νικῶν τὴν μάχην Σφριγᾷ τε καθαρῶς, καὶ σοβεῖ, καὶ τέρπεται· [Alektryōn men toi ge nikōn tēn machēn Sphriga te katharōs, kai sobei, kai terpetai] [II, 685] The cock, when he is the winner in the fight, simply swells, and struts with pomp and exults. And Basil, in the Hexaëmeron, Homily 8: Γαῦρον ὁ ἀλεκτρυὼν, Φιλόκαλον ὁ ταὼς, λάγναι αἱ περιστεραί· [Gauron ho alektryōn, Philokalon ho taōs, lagnai hai peristerai] The cock is a proud thing, the peacock fond of elegance, doves lustful. Lucilius, book 8 of the Satires:
When the victorious barnyard cock has raised himself handsomely onto his toes and lifts up the tips of his claws.

To this, then, belongs the Chaldee and Syriac ܐܒܟܐ abacha, by which I would think not just any cock is meant, but a cock that carries itself thus; and there is added by way of explanation (ἐπεξηγητικῶς [epexēgētikōs]) ܕܡܙܕܪܟܠ ܒܝܢܬ ܬܪܢܓܘܠܬܐ, which struts proudly among the hens. To strut proudly is in Arabic درقل [darqala] darkala, and in Syriac ܕܪܟܠ, whence that ܕܡܙܕܪܟܠ in the Syriac version, which was without doubt taken from the Chaldee. For Elias cites it thus in the Methurgeman: ואכבא דמזדרכיל. But in our editions it is wrongly read דמזרז, which is girded. Those, that is, who supervised the edition corrupted a word they did not understand, substituting another that was closer to the Hebrew. But one must restore דמזדרכל, which struts proudly. For in this place the Targum follows not the Hebrews but the Greek translators, and that דמזדרכל corresponds exactly to the Greek words ἐμπεριπατῶν εὐψύχως [emperipatōn eupsychōs]. There were also others among the ancients who thought a cock is treated here. Among them are Aquila and Theodotion, who had ἀλεκτρυὼν νώτῳ [alektryōn nōtō], a cock with the back, with no sense, or an obscure one. And Jerome, in whom we read a cock girded about the loins. Yet among the Hebrews there is scarcely anyone who refers this place to the cock. And others understand the Gallic dog, or greyhound, which
— — tightly girds the flanks of its belly;

as we have it in the Cynegeticon of Grattius. Others prefer the leopard, which is itself slender about the flanks, as though girded, and walks magnificently. Others the bee, because of the incisions of its abdomen. Others the starling, which in Arabic is called زرزور [zarzūr] zarzur, and in the Talmud זרזיר zarzir. But no one is wiser than Solomon [Jarchi], who admits that he does not know what it is; and Aben Ezra, who says only that it is the name of a beast. As for me, although I defer greatly to so many ancients who would have the cock described here, I see no reason that drove them to that opinion. Nor could the Greeks, who led the way for the others in this rendering, interpret it of the cock except by substituting for the Hebrew words that have nothing in common with it. For the Hebrew means literally girded in the loins, but the Greek something quite different, namely a cock strutting briskly among the females; and these are as far apart as two octaves (δὶς διὰ πασῶν [dis dia pasōn]). Accordingly Symmachus, bidding that cock fly away, rendered περιεσφιγμένον τὴν ὀσφὺν [periesphigmenon tēn osphyn] (for so it should be read, not περιεσφραγισμένον [periesphragismenon]). And Jerome, to reconcile both versions in some fashion, [II, 686] a cock girded about the loins. But what else was this (be it said with all respect to so great a man) than κλώθειν τὰ ἀσύγκλωστα, καὶ τὰ ἀσύστατα συνάπτειν [klōthein ta asynklōsta, kai ta asystata synaptein]? For it does not belong to the description of the cock to say that it has girded loins. And their claim that the cock is so contrasted with the capon is beside the point. For just as a capon is not said to have ungirded loins, so no one would say a cock has girded loins. Granted, though not conceded, that girded in the loins in Hebrew idiom is opposed to castrated: it will not follow that a cock is meant by that name rather than any other animal equally whole and uncastrated. Moreover, since Solomon places the one girded in the loins between the lion and the he-goat, it is very likely that a quadruped, not a bird, is designated by that name. I therefore more willingly side with those who understand the horse [col. 118] here, an animal of proud gait and whose loins are customarily girded, as was said in its place [vol. 1, book 2, ch. 6, p. 103, ss. 40. 41 of this edition]. However that may be, this at least is certain: here too there is nothing that can with certainty be referred to the cock.

XI. The eleventh passage is Eccles. XII, 4. (var. 6.), where it is said of the old man, He shall rise up at the voice of the bird. The Greeks understand the song of sparrows, others of little birds, others finally of cocks. These last would have it mean that the old man is woken at cockcrow, that is, very early in the morning. But the former, that he sleeps so lightly that his sleep is broken at the slightest noise, say at the voice of a sparrow or some other little bird. And they deny that the cock can be meant, because the Hebrew הצפור means only sparrows, or the smallest little birds. That this is utterly false I shall show in its place. So, as far as I am concerned, it may be interpreted either way.

XII. The twelfth passage is Es. XXII, 17, where the Prophet says to Shebna, יהוה מטלטלך טלטלה גבר, The Lord will carry you away with a carrying away, O man. Others render with the carrying away of a man, that is, they say, a manly, strong, vehement one. But this version has two drawbacks. The first is that no example of this expression is adduced. For when we read elsewhere of the way of a man, the sorrow of a man, the redemption of a man, the teaching of a man, no one understands vehemence. We only infer from it that these things either are in a man or proceed from a man. Thus the carrying away of a man would be nothing but that by which a man carries away or is carried away, which would be very weak. Besides, the carrying away of a man would be expressed in Hebrew as טלטלת גבר, not טלטלה. For who would grant what some assert here, that the final He in טלטלה is epenthetic and not the mark of the feminine, since this too is without example? Finally, the accent tiphcha on טלטלה suspends the voice and prevents it from being joined with the following גבר. Clearly, then, גבר is in the vocative case, as if it read אתה הגבר, O you man. This Aben Ezra and Kimchi rightly observed. And long before them the Syriac translator, who has: ܡܪܝܐ ܡܛܠܛܠ ܠܟ ܛܘܠܛܠܐ ܓܒܪܐ, The Lord will surely cast you out, O man. Yet there are some among the Hebrews who render, The Lord will carry you away with the carrying away [II, 687] of a man, or even with the carrying away of a cock. For although the word גבר, very frequent in Scripture, everywhere else means man, here they chose to do violence to the sacred text and interpret it as cock, compelled by no necessity but only by an itch and bad habit of καινοτομία [kainotomia]. Hence on the words טלטלה גבר R. Selomo has כהדין תרנגולא דמטלטל מאתר לאתר, Like a cock that is carried from place to place. This is taken from the Midrash on the Psalms, as Kimchi observes. Accordingly Jerome here has: The Lord will make you be carried off, as a cock is carried off. This, of course, follows the view of that Jew from whom he had learned Hebrew letters, as he himself notes in his Notes, where he paraphrases (παραφράζει [paraphrazei]) this passage thus: And I say this, that you should not labour at hewing out a sepulchre, because the Lord will transfer your priesthood, as גבר is wont to be transferred, which all have interpreted as man. But the Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament translated it cock. “As (he says) a cock is transferred from one place to another on the shoulder of a carrier, so the Lord will lightly carry you away from your place”. Accordingly in the Talmud גבר is sometimes used for cock, as when they say קריאת הגבר for cockcrow. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, p. 67b, גברית is the same as תרנגלת, hen. Indeed, among the paraphrasts Jonathan calls Ezion-geber כרך תרנגולא, the fortress of the cock, Num. XXXIII, 35. 36. and Deut. II, 8., as if Ezion-geber were named from a cock, whereas עציון גבר is the spine of a man. That Ezion-geber was called by this name we have shown in our Phaleg, p. 764, because it is situated in a place inaccessible because of reefs and rocks (ῥαχίαις καὶ σπίλοις ἀπροσίτῳ [rhachiais kai spilois aprositō]), like Dyrrachium in Macedonia. And what is read of Balaam in Num. XXIV, 3., נאם הגבר, The man said, Baal Hatturim takes as if it read The cock said, and taking occasion [col. 119] from this he draws a ridiculous comparison of Balaam with a cock in these words: קרא גבר שדומה בלעם לתרנגול כמו שהתרנגול הוא נואף מכל כן בלעם רבע אתונו וכמו שהתרנגול יודע בעתים כן בלעם יודע לכוין השעה שהקב״ה כועס וכמו שהתרנגול דרכו לעמוד על רגל אחד כן בלעם חגר באחד רגליו, He calls him גבר, because Balaam was like a cock. As the cock is lecherous above all, so Balaam lay with his she-ass; as the cock knows the times, so Balaam knew how to find out the hour at which God, the Holy One, blessed be He, is angry; as the cock is wont to stand on one foot, so Balaam was lame in one foot. Most absurd of all is this: although the other sacrifices which God had prescribed in his Law have now been abolished, yet on the day preceding the feast of Atonement there is no one among the Jews who does not offer a cock for himself, repeating these words while he strikes it against his head three times: זה חליפתי זה תחתי זה כפרתי זה התרנגול ילך למיתה ואני אלך לחיים טובים עם ירשאל אמן, Let this cock be an exchange for me; let this be in my place; let this be an atonement for me; let this cock go to death, but I, with all Israel, to a happy life. Amen. For the rest, consult the distinguished Buxtorf's Synagoga, chapter 20. Here it suffices to add that the occasion of the error was the ambiguous word גבר, by which they hold that both man and cock are signified. It is fitting, therefore, they say, that since גבר has sinned, גבר [II, 688] should bear the penalty of the sin. As if a cock and a man could be held as one before God's tribunal because, through an abuse of the word, they are called by the same name. I deliberately pass over what is found about the cock in the second Targum of Esther, because these are not paraphrases but the author's mere fabrications.

notes.text: More probable is the view of SELDEN (de Diis Syris, Syntagma 2, ch. 7), that these were the huts of the daughters, in which daughters prostituted their virginity at the temple of Venus Mylitta; see Herodotus, book 1, §. 199; Strabo, book 16, p. 1081, ed. Almeloveen.

But since in none of the other dialects is the hen called by the name זגתא, Michaelis, in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1902, can hardly persuade himself that it was so called in Chaldee. In Arabic زجّ [zujj] is the extremity of a thing, the iron at the lower end of a spear, and then the pole, or the pivot around which a millstone turns. Hence Michaelis thinks it probable that זגתא is the pole star. But that most learned man did not consider that in the very passage of the Chaldee version with which we are dealing, a meaning other than hen can hardly have a place, since אפרחתא is immediately added to זגתא. If, then, you take זגתא here in the sense Michaelis devised, this charming rendering will result: and will you lead the pole star with her chicks? Moreover, Michaelis wrongly disregards the use of the word זגתא in the Talmud, confusing the Talmudic writers, who write fairly pure Chaldee, with the later Rabbis. To the authority of the latter, indeed, no one will attribute anything in establishing meanings; but the usage of the Chaldee dialect was certainly well known to those older writers.

Niebuhr also testifies that not only the Jews of Sanaa and Baghdad, but also the Arabs living on the Persian Gulf call the Great Bear Asch. In the Descript. Arab. p. 114 he relates that a Jew of Sanaa, an astrologer but unskilled in knowledge of the stars, when questioned by him, answered after consulting other Jews that Asch is Om ennäsch, the Great Bear. P. 115: Näsch, or Benäth Näsch, which constellation the Jews at Sanaa and Baghdad, as well as the Arabs on the Persian Gulf, also call Asch, is the Great Bear.

Schultens, in his Commentary on this passage of Job, holds that the Hebrew עיש should be referred to the Arabic عوس [ʿws] and عسّ [ʿass] to go round by night, whence عاسّ [ʿāss] a night watchman walking through cities. For both Bears, never setting and wandering about in the sky through the whole night, could be excellently compared to such a night watchman. Although Michaelis follows this in the Supplemm. p. 1907, it displeases me, chiefly because it smacks of etymological subtleties, whereas we see that in naming celestial signs it was not so much etymological reasons that were considered as resemblances to other things whose forms and shapes they most nearly approached. Nor am I moved by what Schultens and Michaelis object to Bochart's view, that Hebrew ש usually corresponds not to Arabic ش but to س, since not a few words exist in which ש and ش correspond to each other; Schultens himself collected several in the Clavis Dialector. p. 300, 301.
